articles.title: Delivery of first Dhruv NG helicopters to Pawan Hans a big milestone, says HAL CMD as PSU approaches states for civil aviation push
articles.summary: News News: BENGALURU: September 18 is a historic day for India's elite aerospace and defence organisation Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. On Friday, the elite pub.
articles.body: BENGALURU: September 18 is a historic day for India's elite aerospace and defence organisation Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. On Friday, the elite public sector undertaking chairman and managing director Ravi K is going to hand over the first batch of four Dhruv New Generation civil helicopters to Pawan Hans Limited in the presence of Union civil aviation minister Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu. Defence minister Rajnath Singh and Indian Air Force chief Air Chief Marshal A P Singh will also be present at the ceremony as it is a big day for the Indian Air Force too. The IAF will also get the delivery of the last two Tejas Mk 1 trainer aircraft of the first contact of 40 LCA jets and the long-pending trainer aircraft HTT-40 from HAL on Friday evening.“In the evening, I will be in Bengaluru (Karnataka) to attend the handing over ceremony of LCA Tejas FOC Twin Seater Trainers & HTT 40 Basic Trainer Aircraft to Indian Air Force and Dhruv NG helicopters to Pawan Hans Ltd. Looking forward to it,” defence minister Rajnath Singh said in a morning post on X on Friday.Dhruv NG helicopter is a 5.5-tonne, light twin-engine, multi-role helicopter, which can perform several functions like it can be used for UDAN regional connectivity service, offshore operations, casualty evacuation, tourism, disaster management, underslung cargo, search and rescue, mining and exploration. The Dhruv NG is based on HAL's Advanced Light Helicopter programme and has lots of additional features.With an endurance of 3 hours and 40 minutes and service ceiling of 6,000 metres, Dhruv NG can fly at 285 km/h speed and can carry up to 14 passengers. The first delivery of four Dhruv NG helicopters to Pawan Hans on Friday will also establish HAL as a manufacturer of an advanced civilian helicopter. Pawan Hans had ordered 10 Dhruv NG helicopters in Jan. The remaining six are expected to be delivered by Dec.HAL CMD Ravi K told TOI, “Dhruv NG is a multirole civilian helicopter as it can perform various functions. Key among them are offshore duties as well as medivac. It is a milestone not only for all of us at HAL but also for the country.”HAL is approaching state govts to pitch its Dhruv NG helicopter for civilian applications. According to HAL, most states have shown interest in the civilian helicopter.HAL currently derives around 5% of its turnover from non-military business and the company aims to raise this share to 25% over the next decade. HAL estimates that India could require around 400 such civilian helicopters in the Dhruv NG category in the coming years.

articles.title: In 1995, a broken sewer line and heavy rain opened a 250-foot-wide San Francisco sinkhole that swallowed a three-storey Tudor house, trees and utility poles
articles.summary: US News: Explore the shocking 1995 San Francisco sinkhole incident where a powerful storm and aging sewer infrastructure led to the dramatic collapse of a Tudor house in the affluent Sea Cliff neighborhood, revealing the city's ongoing struggles with its aging sewer system.
articles.body: In December 1995, a century-old brick sewer ruptured beneath San Francisco’s Sea Cliff neighborhood during heavy rain, sending water into the surrounding ground and creating a rapidly expanding sinkhole. Beneath its serene streets is a system of sewer mains, many of which were constructed of brick and installed over a century ago, long before anybody could have predicted the amount of stormwater the city would eventually have to manage.An old pipe under pressureA strong rainstorm struck the Bay Area on December 11, 1995, with an intensity that was exceptional for the region but not unprecedented. A brick sewer line was constructed around the turn of the century under Sea Cliff, and as rainfall coursed through the system, an overflow structure about 1400 feet farther down the line constricted the flow and caused pressure to build up within the ageing pipe. A forensic analysis published later by Missouri University of Science and Technology determined that water had begun to push its way into gaps in the sewer wall, fissures that were likely enlarged years before by construction work performed under the pipe. The fissures began opening up further as the surrounding dirt of the cracked sewer lost its confinement until the pipe burst totally, sending a torrent of water straight into the surrounding earth.A house disappears into the groundThe escaping water eroded a hole that grew to more than 250 feet wide and about 40 feet deep, undermining the unoccupied Tudor-style home at 125 El Camino Del Mar, which had been offered for sale in 1993 for $2.6 million. The three-story Tudor home at 125 El Camino Del Mar slid into the crater as the soil beneath it gave way. The neighborhood’s exposure is no stranger to geologists either. Steep, weakly packed terrain nearby had been identified by the US Geological Survey as vulnerable to rapid failure in its mapping of landslide-prone territory in the greater San Francisco Bay region. By late that day, at least 23 other houses and an apartment building had been evacuated as the unstable ground threatened nearby properties. The destroyed house at 125 El Camino Del Mar also bordered the former boyhood home of photographer Ansel Adams at 129 24th Avenue. Nobody was hurt, but the financial and structural cost was high, and the vacant gated lot it left behind was an eyesore in the community for years to come.A citywide infrastructure issueMany of the mains in San Francisco’s combined sewer system, which carries both wastewater and stormwater in the same pipes, are over a hundred years old. Since then, the San Francisco Water Power Sewer has acknowledged that routine repairs alone cannot keep up with a network of this age. The agency has spent years working through a multi-billion dollar programme aimed at replacing and reinforcing ageing brick sewers throughout the city, including parts not far from where the 1995 collapse occurred. But for Sea Cliff homeowners, the events of December 1995 were a sobering lesson in how one storm, meeting a pipe already compromised by age, can destabilize a residential neighborhood within hours.The lot where the house once stood remained undeveloped after the collapse. The 1995 disaster also became an example of how failures in aging sewer infrastructure can interact with heavy rainfall and unstable ground. San Francisco continues to upgrade its more than century-old combined sewer system as part of its broader infrastructure program.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2024, Horry County placed about 200 wire baskets of recycled oyster shells along Garden City’s Atlantic Avenue to build a living reef
articles.summary: US News: In 2024, Horry County initiated a project to combat shoreline erosion in Garden City, South Carolina, by constructing a living reef with 200 wire baskets of recycled oyster shells. This eco-friendly solution supports marine life and enhances water quality while protecting the coastline from harsh environmental factors.
articles.body: For years, the soft banks that shield the marsh below Garden City, South Carolina, have been steadily eroded by boat wakes, tides, and more regular storms. In 2024, Horry County used a different strategy that begins with something that most people would typically toss in the trash rather than using concrete or rock to hold the queue. The county started putting wire baskets packed with recycled oyster shells into the marsh along Atlantic Avenue, in collaboration with state wildlife officials, creating what is essentially a live reef that can simultaneously develop, filter water, and delay erosion.Shells turned back into the shoreAccording to Horry County, the idea uses oyster shells left from restaurants and backyard gatherings around the county that would otherwise go to a landfill. When cured, the shells are stacked into wire cages called constructed wire reefs and lowered into the marsh, where they produce a solid textured surface for new oyster larvae to settle on. In 2024, the county put up about 200 of the baskets along Atlantic Avenue in Garden City as part of a larger effort to use recycled material to fight marsh erosion rather than importing stone or concrete. In the years since, county personnel have added further baskets to the reef, built with support from local high school students and others.Why oysters are the best building blocksOyster larvae prefer to settle on other oyster shells rather than on rock, sand, or plastic, making old shells particularly effective for culturing. The scientific term for this kind of hard nesting substrate is cultch. The South Carolina Department of Natural Resources says a persistent problem along the coastline is a lack of oyster shell to use in this type of habitat restoration. That is why the state encourages residents, restaurants and event organisers to recycle their shells instead of tossing them away. As baby oysters attach to the baskets, they begin filtering the surrounding water, and one adult oyster is estimated to filter dozens of gallons of water in a day, as the reef itself gets denser and more efficient at soaking up wave energy over time. A healthy oyster reef is, in essence, self-reinforcing, generating new shells and new structures quicker than storms and currents can erode it, if the population within it remains healthy. This type of nature-based coastline protection has been gaining popularity well beyond South Carolina, for reasons that go beyond cost.A gentler option than concreteTraditional shoreline defences such as bulkheads and seawalls establish a hard, immovable barrier between land and water but can also exacerbate erosion nearby and offer nothing in the way of habitat for fish, crabs or birds. Living shorelines, made with natural materials such as oyster shell, tend to be cheaper to construct and maintain than rigid structures, and they improve water quality and support far more marine species in the process, according to NOAA Fisheries. A seawall is built to a set height and stays there. A living coastline, however, can change and expand over time. It can slowly increase in height as sediment builds up. For a stretch of coastline like Garden City, where the marsh behind Atlantic Avenue depends on a stable edge to survive, that adaptability could prove just as valuable as the erosion control itself, and Horry County has already signalled plans to keep expanding the reef in the years ahead, one recycled shell at a time.Beyond the reef itself, the project also gives ordinary citizens a direct way to participate in something that can otherwise feel abstract. Anyone who throws a bag of shells into a local recycling bin after a family dinner is, in fact, supplying raw material for the next basket that ends up in the marsh. County authorities have said the goal is to close that loop completely so that every oyster eaten locally can eventually make its way back into the water as habitat for the next generation. As they age, and as oysters begin to colonise them, the baskets should gradually form a more resilient and more diverse stretch of beach along Atlantic Avenue than has been the case for years, made from shells that would otherwise have been thrown away, rather than imported stone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A 12-year-old North Carolina girl rescued 114 stuffed animals from thrift stores; she repaired every one by hand and donated them to children who lost their homes in fire
articles.summary: US News: A trip to a thrift store can often end with an impulse purchase or two, but for one 12-year-old girl in North Carolina, finding discarded stuffed anim.
articles.body: A trip to a thrift store can often end with an impulse purchase or two, but for one 12-year-old girl in North Carolina, finding discarded stuffed animals became the beginning of a much bigger mission. Instead of seeing worn-out toys as things that had reached the end of their lives, the young girl saw something that could be repaired and given a second chance. Over time, she collected 114 stuffed animals from thrift stores, cleaned and repaired them by hand and eventually donated them to children who had lost their homes in fires.Her story, shared by the American Red Cross on Instagram, offers a glimpse into how a simple idea by a child turned into an effort to bring comfort to other children during some of the most difficult moments of their lives.From thrift-store shelves to a child's handsStuffed animals are often among the belongings children attach to early in life. A worn teddy bear, rabbit or other soft toy can become a familiar companion, making the loss of one during a house fire particularly painful for a child. This is why American Red Cross responders often carry stuffed animals to provide comfort and reassurance after a disaster.Earlier this summer, as supplies began running low following an increase in home fires across the area, Disaster Program Manager Jon McCollum asked the community for help.Sadie Hutson, a resident of Dubson, North Carolina, answered the call and soon, began collecting such toys from thrift stores rather than leaving them behind. But buying them was only the first step. She repaired each of the 114 stuffed animals herself. The toys that might have otherwise remained on thrift-store shelves or been discarded were cleaned, mended and restored before being prepared for their next homes.Her project was not simply about collecting toys. It was about transforming something old into something that could offer comfort to another child.Why stuffed animals can matter after a disasterFor children who lose their homes in fires, the damage can extend far beyond walls, furniture and possessions. Familiar objects, photographs, school supplies and toys can disappear within minutes. While emergency organisations work to provide necessities such as food, shelter, clothing and other assistance, small personal items can also provide a sense of familiarity during a period of upheaval.That is where the girl's project takes on particular significance. A repaired stuffed animal may seem like a small gift compared with the scale of what a family loses in a fire. But for a child suddenly surrounded by unfamiliar places and routines, having something soft and familiar to hold can offer a moment of comfort. "Hearing the stories was a little heartbreaking," Sadie said. "That's why I did it."The 114 toys therefore had a journey of their own. They moved from thrift-store shelves, into the hands of a 12-year-old who carefully repaired them, and finally toward children who needed something comforting after losing their homes.A second life for 114 toysThere is also an environmental side to the project. Stuffed animals that have been used or damaged are not always easy to donate directly. By repairing them instead of treating them as disposable items, the girl extended the useful life of each toy.Her approach follows a simple principle of reuse: something that looks worn or unwanted does not necessarily have to be thrown away. The project also demonstrates how charitable efforts do not always require large sums of money or sophisticated resources. In this case, the contribution involved thrift-store finds, time, patience and the willingness to repair 114 individual toys.In recognition of her efforts, Jon and fellow volunteers recently presented Sadie with the Young Humanitarian Award at the Central Surry Volunteer Fire Department. "A lot of times children get overlooked in the initial, chaotic stages of a disaster," Jon said. "We want to make sure they are taken care of immediately as well."According to Hutson, "As long as you do it through the kindness of your heart, you can do it," she said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kohat: At least 16 killed in attack on mosque in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
articles.summary: A vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque building during Friday prayers, a senior police official says.
articles.body:
At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar.

A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way.

In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion."

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack", according to Reuters news agency.

There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.

Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast.

Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police.

Islamabad says militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies the accusation and says militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Social media influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj was released from Tihar Jail late Thursday night, three days after a Delhi court granted him three weeks' interim bail in connection with the alleged assault on the father of a student activist during a protest at Jantar Mantar, officials said on Friday.A video showed Bhardwaj quickly moving towards a waiting car outside the jail before leaving with his associates.On September 15, a Delhi court granted Bhardwaj interim bail for three weeks and said it would consider his plea for regular bail after observing his conduct during the period.The sessions court imposed several conditions while granting him relief. articles.title: We have duty to 'progress' Good Friday Agreement, Micheál Martin tells Andy Burnham
articles.summary: The pair were expected to discuss a further strengthening of ties including boosting trade, security and working with the European Union.
articles.body:
Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin has told Prime Minister Andy Burnham their governments have a duty to "mind and progress" the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.

Burnham said the relationship between the UK and Ireland matters "on every single level" as they met at Number 10 North for talks on Friday.

The pair were expected to discuss a further strengthening of ties including boosting trade, security and working with the European Union.

The prime minister said they were "working together" to uphold the principles of the peace deal for Northern Ireland.

Speaking ahead of their talks, Burnham said it "feels very fitting" to welcome Martin as the first international visitor to Number 10 North in Manchester.

"The relationship between the UK and Ireland matters so much on every single level," he said.

Burnham added that as "co-custodians of the Good Friday Agreement, we are working together to uphold its principles as we approach the 30th anniversary".

The Good Friday Agreement, also known as the Belfast Agreement, was a political deal designed to bring an end to 30 years of violent conflict in Northern Ireland, known as the Troubles.

The taoiseach expressed his sympathies with Burnham following the recent death of his father .

Martin said he appreciated the meeting going ahead, telling the prime minister: "I think your sense of duty shines through."

The taoiseach said "in a global world marked by uncertainty" it was "important that two close neighbours continue the very strong engagement".

He added: "We are co-guarantors of the Good Friday Agreement. We have very significant obligations to mind it and to progress it and so forth."

Martin said he was also looking forward to discussing "even stronger and closer relationships between the European Union and the United Kingdom, which will be of benefit to the European Union and to Ireland".

A Downing Street spokesperson said the two leaders began by "reaffirming the close partnership between the UK and Ireland, as well as their shared commitment to upholding the Good Friday Agreement".

They also discussed the legacy of the Troubles and "working towards lasting reconciliation in Northern Ireland".

Other topics included the UK's closer relationship with Europe, their joint support for Ukraine, and looked ahead the UK's hosting of the next UK-Ireland Summit next year.

articles.title: 'Will go to any extent': Pakistan pledges to defend Saudi Arabia amid Houthi threat
articles.summary: Middle East News: Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi Arabia 'to any extent', with its military spokesperson saying Islamabad would support the kingdom “both diplomati.
articles.body: Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi Arabia 'to any extent', with its military spokesperson saying Islamabad would support the kingdom “both diplomatically and physically” amid heightened tensions involving Yemen's Houthi forces.In an interview with Arab News on Thursday, Pakistan's military spokesperson Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Islamabad remained committed to Saudi Arabia's security.“We will go to any extent for the security of (the two holy sanctuaries) and the kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” he said.“Pakistan fully stands with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, both diplomatically and physically,” Chaudhry told Arab News.His remarks came after Saudi Arabia reported intercepting a Houthi drone near Mecca earlier this week. Riyadh said the drone was destroyed south of the holy city before entering prohibited airspace.Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree, however, rejected the allegation that the group had targeted Islamic holy sites, saying its operations were directed at Saudi oil facilities and military bases.Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif had earlier said there was “absolutely no ambiguity” over Islamabad's obligations under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye last month.Speaking to Geo News on Wednesday, Asif said, “Mecca Agreement applies to us, and we will fulfil our duty.”He said Pakistan's responsibility to protect the Muslim holy sites existed independently of the agreement.“If Mecca is attacked, there is no need for an agreement to protect it,” Asif added.Asif said the agreement provides for collective defence if the territorial integrity or geographical boundaries of any of its three signatories are violated. He declined to disclose details of Pakistan's potential military response, saying such matters would not be discussed publicly.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif also reiterated Pakistan's support for Saudi Arabia, saying Islamabad stood “shoulder to shoulder” with Riyadh. He condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous attempted drone attack” and called for restraint.The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement was signed on August 7, in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif. The three-way pact was signed against a backdrop of wider regional tensions, including conflict involving the United States and Iran and attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sea Mills mother expected to plead guilty to killing children
articles.summary: Yasmeen Ali is expected to plead guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.
articles.body:
A mother is expected to plead guilty to killing her three young children, a court has heard.

Seven-year-old Fares Bash, three-year-old Joury Bash and nine-month-old Mohammed Bash died at their home in Sea Mills, Bristol, on 18 February 2024.

Yasmeen Ali, 44, is expected to plead guilty to their manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility, and the infanticide of her nine-month-old son.

An inquest previously heard that the three children died of knife wounds, with injuries to their chests and necks. Fares Bash also showed possible signs of asphyxia.

Ali, of no fixed address, is currently charged with three counts of murder and was due to face trial next month at Bristol Crown Court.

Anna Vigars KC, prosecuting, told the court earlier that two psychiatrists had prepared reports which had made the reduced pleas available.

"As the court will be aware we have received two psychiatric reports," she said.

"Both of them, perhaps unsurprisingly in the circumstances of this case, indicating that the partial defence of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility is available to Ms Ali.

"The third count, as far as infanticide is concerned, that's simply because of the youngest child's age at the time of his death.

"The defence of diminished responsibility applies to all three deaths.

"Having been able to spend some time with the children's father, Mr Alfil Bash, and to explain the position to him, I am in the position to indicate to the court that were those pleas to be forthcoming they are pleas that would be accepted by the Crown."

Andrew Langdon KC, defending, told the court he was due to speak with the defendant in the coming weeks but expected the guilty pleas to be formally entered at the next hearing.

"We are grateful for that indication, and our position is that we anticipate that guilty pleas to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility in relation to all three of the children will be entered," he said.

"There isn't going to be a trial is our confident prediction."

Mr Justice Linden scheduled the next hearing for 23 October, when the case is expected to conclude.

Ali, who was not required to appear at the hearing, is being held in a secure psychiatric hospital.

Following the incident, Avon and Somerset Police referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct over prior contact but the watchdog said no investigation was required.

articles.title: ‘Unconstitutional, illegal, undemocratic’: Mamata after EC assigns new symbol and name
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee on Friday called the developments surrounding the Trinamool Congress’ internal factional .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee on Friday called the developments surrounding the Trinamool Congress’ internal factional dispute a “black day” in India’s democratic history, after her camp’s Nandigram bypoll candidate withdrew her nomination.Addressing a press conference, Mamata said her camp did not disrespect the Constitutional Chair but alleged that the developments were “unconstitutional, illegal, undemocratic and a totally biased vendetta to satisfy the ego of a political party”.“We don't disrespect the Constitutional Chair, but we feel today is a black day in our democratic history. What is happening in our country is very unfortunate, unconstitutional, illegal, undemocratic and a totally biased vendetta to satisfy the ego of a political party,” she said.Mamata also alleged that there had been an earlier warning that her faction would not be allowed to retain its party name and symbol.“They had said beforehand, ‘naam bhi rakhne doonga, nishaan bhi nahi rakhne doonga’. Who are these people? They are in power today, they might not be in power tomorrow. They should understand their limitations,” she said.Mamata backs Congress in NandigramThe comments came after Sanchita Pradhan Dey, the Nandigram bypoll candidate of the Mamata Banerjee camp, withdrew her nomination on Friday, a day before the deadline for withdrawal.The development followed an interim Election Commission order freezing the use of the All India Trinamool Congress name and its traditional twin-flowers-on-grass symbol by both rival factions.The EC subsequently allotted the Mamata Banerjee-led faction the name “Mamata All India Trinamool Congress” and the symbol “Football Player”, to be treated as a recognised political party in West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura.The group led by Arup Roy was allotted the name “Democratic Trinamool Congress” and the symbol “Envelope”.Dey had filed her nomination from Nandigram as the candidate of the Mamata Banerjee-led faction, accompanied by former state minister Akhil Giri.Earlier on Friday, Dey also met West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari in Kolkata.With Saturday being the last date for withdrawal of nominations, the meeting came amid the reshaping of the electoral contest.Mamata said her camp would now support the Congress in Nandigram as well as Assam.""They do not know that I cannot leave All India Trinamool Congress. It will always be with me until I leave this world...Absolutely dirty game but we are also ready to fight it out. I want the BJP to go from India. We want solidarity in INDI Alliance...In Nandigram, we are going to give our support to Congress party. It is for the greater interest of the country. Rejinagar, I will decide later. In Assam, we are not contesting..."," she said.Mamata alleges ‘vote theft’Speaking about what she described as “vote theft”, Mamata accused the BJP of undermining democratic institutions and said the issue was a matter of “great sadness”."It is a matter of great sadness. They looted in Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Bengal. This 'Jhootha BJP Party', a 'Jumla Party'...Its job is to end democracy, Constitution and education system in the country. Even journalists are not spared; if someone speaks out against them, they are arrested. Before us, Uddhav Thackeray faced the same thing. I have no respect for any individual person who is busy only to satisfy the ego of BJP..." she said.The developments follow the Election Commission’s interim order that froze the use of the Trinamool Congress’ traditional name and symbol by both factions, resulting in separate names and symbols being assigned to the rival groups.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Pakistan security crisis deepens: Nearly 1,000 forces killed in 9 months
articles.summary: International News: With fatalities among security personnel crossing the 1,000 mark, 2026 is turning out to be one of the deadliest years in Pakistan since the South Asi.
articles.body: With fatalities among security personnel crossing the 1,000 mark, 2026 is turning out to be one of the deadliest years in Pakistan since the South Asian Terrorism Portal (SATP) began keeping records in 2000. In terms of fatalities among security forces, which include the army, Frontier Corps (FC) and police (including levies), Pakistan's security situation continues to deteriorate, with the country recording over a thousand violent incidents between January 1 and September 15, 2026, according to SATP. More than 650 civilians were killed in terrorist and other violent incidents in the same time frame. After 2025 and 2009, with 1,012 security forces fatalities, this is the third deadliest year for Pakistani forces so far.As per the data compiled by the portal, 2009 was the deadliest year in Pakistan, in which 11,317 people were killed in violent militant incidents. Since then the numbers have come down, although there has been a significant rise in 2025, with 4,001 fatalities reported. Up to September 15 of this year, 3,693 fatalities have been reported. As per the figures available, nearly 78,000 individuals, including militants, have been killed in these violent incidents.Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa have emerged as the principal theatres of violence, with insurgent groups repeatedly targeting security installations, convoys and government facilities. In August alone, around 190 attacks were reported, followed by about 15 incidents in the first five days of September, according to the report. The figures underline the scale of the challenge facing Islamabad as it attempts to contain multiple militant threats across its western provinces.Incidents of violence have been on the rise after a brief period of relative calm from 2018 to 2022. They have continued rising since 2022, just a year after the Taliban took over Afghanistan. An offshoot of the Taliban, known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, has since been fighting to unite the Pashtun areas on both sides of the Durand Line, the border between the two countries. The line, named after Sir Henry Mortimer Durand, was created after the Second Anglo-Afghan War and has been a bone of contention, first between Afghanistan and the British Empire, then between Kabul and Islamabad. The TTP also wants to establish Sharia rule in the areas it seeks to govern in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan.Another area of great concern for the Pakistanis is the restive province of Balochistan. This resource-rich province has been in the news for years over large-scale terror attacks by Baloch insurgents. The Baloch have been attacking rail and road infrastructure across the province, carrying out Improvised Explosive Device (IED) attacks and ambushes. The Baloch insurgents have also carried out multiple attacks on the Jaffar Express, which connects the provincial capital of Quetta with the rest of the country.

articles.title: Meet the brother-sister duo who built a Bolivian snack brand during the COVID; the business is now targeting $500,000 in revenue
articles.summary: US News: Carlos and Christina Schenstrom turned a long-standing idea into a business when the pandemic gave them time to revisit their dream of bringing a tast.
articles.body: Carlos and Christina Schenstrom turned a long-standing idea into a business when the pandemic gave them time to revisit their dream of bringing a taste of Bolivia to the US. In 2021, the brother and sister launched Cassavida, a snack company centred on cuñapés, a traditional Bolivian bite made with cassava starch and cheese. In an interview with Entrepreneur, the siblings said the business is now targeting $500,000 in revenue for 2026 after a rebrand and entry into Sprouts program in 2025. What started without experience in the US food industry has since become a full-time venture.How did the siblings build their Bolivian snack brand during the pandemicThe idea for Cassavida had been discussed by Carlos and Christina since their college years at the University of Kansas. They had wanted to introduce American consumers to Bolivian food, and cuñapés stood out as a natural starting point.The snack is small, crunchy and cheesy, and is made using cassava and artisan cheese. The official website of Cassavida describes it as a food that reflects the company’s wider aim of introducing people to Bolivia through its flavours and culinary traditions. The website reports that Bolivia’s food culture contains many traditions that remain relatively unknown outside the country.When the pandemic slowed their normal routines, the siblings decided to finally pursue the idea. Neither of them had experience in consumer food products or the US snack market, but they began building the business anyway.The early business required a much larger investmentThe first steps involved finding advisers who could help the siblings understand an unfamiliar industry. The siblings said in the interview with Entrepreneur that branding became an early focus for them, while the initial investment was about $200,000.By 2023, they recognised that building the business would require considerably more money and resources. They later worked with California-based agency Dayjob on a rebrand and also built their own manufacturing facility in Bolivia.The siblings told Entrepreneur that they had invested just under $1 million in bringing Cassavida to life. The scale of that investment shows how different turning a food idea into a functioning brand can be from simply creating a product at home.What makes Cassavida different from an ordinary snack brandCassavida is built around more than the snack itself. On its website, the company says its mission is to introduce people to what it describes as Bolivia’s unexpected greatness, beginning with food.The company also highlights the farms behind some of its ingredients. Cassavida website reports that it supports small family farms and regenerative agricultural practices, including dairy farming where cows can move freely, remain with their calves and eat naturally on grass rather than relying on grain as a substitute.The product range has also expanded beyond the original cheese version. The company currently lists Classic Cheese, Rosemary Garlic, Spicy Andean Ají varieties and more. The Spicy Andean Ají version uses locoto pepper, which Cassavida says has been used in the Andes for generations.The 2025 rebrand changed the business trajectoryA major turning point came in mid-2025, when the siblings relaunched the company following its rebrand and entered Sprouts’ Innovation programme.According to the interview, Cassavida’s annual sales had remained below $50,000 before the relaunch. The business had generated more than $100,000 during 2025 and was projected to finish the year at around $150,000.The change was not simply about getting the snack into more places. The rebranding process helped the siblings better understand the purpose behind the company. They described their broader ambition as becoming an unofficial food tourism board for Bolivia by encouraging pride in the country and curiosity about it abroad.Why the siblings are taking a focused approach to growthCassavida’s expansion has not been based on trying to enter every possible shop at once. Carlos said in the interview that the company prefers to build its presence carefully, beginning in specific regions and working with retailers that fit its product and brand.That approach is particularly important for a young food company because gaining shelf space is only one part of the challenge. The business also needs enough sales to justify remaining there. The siblings said they want to build strong sales in selected locations before expanding further. New opportunities arrived in 2025 through Sprouts and plans to grow across Southern California and online.The Schenstroms have moved from treating Cassavida as a side project to making it their full-time focus. Carlos now spends most of his working week on production, marketing, operations and planning, while Christina focuses on brand strategy, marketing and public relations.The siblings also continue learning about the food industry and meeting other professionals. For Cassavida, the growth is also tied to a larger purpose of putting a distinctly Bolivian snack on more US shelves while giving consumers an introduction to a food tradition they may not have encountered before.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Chan Mathok Atak jailed over Channel boat with 165 migrants
articles.summary: Chan Mathok Atak has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison after piloting the boat.
articles.body:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July.

Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.

At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August.

At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified".

She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence.

James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus.

The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels.

The dinghy, which had 31 children on board with the youngest aged 14, had two outboard engines but one was not working, the court heard.

Harrison said just before the boat was intercepted, Atak moved away from the engine into another part of the vessel and took off his jacket.

He said this was an attempt to not to be identified as the helmsman.

However, Atak was seen during 90 minutes of aerial footage to be piloting the vessel using its one remaining functioning engine, the court heard.

articles.body: Yemen has long been described as the graveyard of Saudi ambition. And this month Riyadh learnt its latest lesson.For more than a decade, the kingdom has spent billions of dollars, deployed advanced weapons and invested enormous political capital in trying to contain the Houthi movement on its southern border. What began as a northern Yemeni insurgency has developed into a formidable military force capable of launching missiles and drones across the region and threatening one of the world's most important shipping routes.The latest setback came this month, when Houthi forces captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and then advanced towards the strategic island of Perim, also known as Mayyun, at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb strait.Mocha was not the whole story. It was the door to a much bigger one.The Houthi advance has brought the group closer to one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints at a time when Saudi Arabia is already dealing with disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on its energy infrastructure. For Riyadh, a war that once looked like a campaign to defeat a relatively weak neighbour has become a problem involving shipping, oil, national security and regional influence.The question is no longer simply why Saudi Arabia has struggled to defeat the Houthis. It is why its enormous military and financial advantages have failed to produce a lasting political and military victory.What is happening nowThe latest escalation comes amid a wider Middle East conflict, with the US and Israel fighting Iran. What we know about the Houthi attack:Mocha falls: Houthi forces captured the Red Sea port of Mocha in September, expanding their control along Yemen's western coast.Perim comes next: The Houthis then moved onto Perim, an island sitting inside the Bab el-Mandeb strait, bringing them closer to a vital global shipping route.Saudi oil routes face pressure: With the Strait of Hormuz disrupted by the wider regional conflict, Saudi Arabia has relied more heavily on its East-West Pipeline to move crude to the Red Sea. The pipeline was subsequently hit by a drone strike linked to Iran-aligned forces elsewhere in the region.The war reaches Saudi Arabia: Houthi missiles and drones have continued to target Saudi territory and energy infrastructure, including the Jazan area. Saudi authorities also reported intercepting a drone approaching the southern sector of Mecca, an incident the Houthis denied was a deliberate attempt to target the holy city.Riyadh has not returned to ground war: Saudi Arabia has responded with air strikes and defensive operations but has so far avoided a major ground intervention.The war that never really endedThe roots of the current crisis go back much further than 2015.The Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, emerged from a Zaydi revivalist movement in northern Yemen during the 1990s. Zaydism is a branch of Shia Islam with deep roots in Yemen, particularly in the country's north.The movement grew partly in opposition to the spread of Saudi-backed Salafi religious influence in Yemen. During the 2000s, the Houthis fought several wars against the Yemeni government and developed a growing military organisation.In 2014, the movement captured Sanaa and forced President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi's government out of the capital. The Houthis then expanded southwards.Saudi Arabia saw the rise of the movement as a direct security threat. A hostile force with links to Iran was now controlling large parts of the country next door.In March 2015, Saudi Arabia assembled a coalition and launched Operation Decisive Storm. The objective was to restore the internationally recognised government and push the Houthis back.The campaign began with overwhelming Saudi and coalition air power. But the expected quick victory never came.Saudi aircraft could destroy weapons depots, command centres and military positions. What they could not do was create a stable political order on the ground. Yemeni forces fighting the Houthis were divided, while the Houthis adapted to the campaign and became increasingly experienced.The war dragged on for years.A UN-brokered truce in 2022 brought a major reduction in fighting. It did not produce a final political settlement. Instead, the conflict entered a period of uneasy calm.For Saudi Arabia, the truce froze a conflict in which the kingdom had failed to restore the Yemeni government to power across the country.Why Saudi Arabia could not turn military power into victorySaudi Arabia has some of the most advanced military equipment in the region. It operates sophisticated US-made fighter aircraft, precision-guided weapons and missile defence systems.Yet the Yemen war exposed a basic problem with military power.An insurgency cannot normally be defeated through air strikes alone.Air power can destroy targets. It cannot hold a town after the bombs stop falling. It cannot build a functioning government, persuade local communities to support an unpopular administration or settle rival political claims.That problem became particularly severe in Yemen because Saudi Arabia did not have a single, unified Yemeni partner capable of taking territory and holding it.Instead, the anti-Houthi camp has been deeply divided.The internationally recognised government has struggled with internal disputes. The Southern Transitional Council, backed by the United Arab Emirates, wants greater autonomy and has long pushed for southern independence. Other forces, including the National Resistance Forces and Islah-linked groups, have their own interests and networks.Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also backed different actors at different points in the war.That rivalry matters because defeating the Houthis requires more than driving them away from a particular battlefield. Someone has to take control afterwards.If the forces fighting the Houthis disagree about what Yemen should look like, military victories become difficult to turn into lasting political gains.The Houthis have benefited from precisely this weakness.They have had years to develop military experience while their opponents have spent much of the same period fighting among themselves.That is one reason the latest loss of territory is significant. The problem is not simply that the Houthis are advancing. It is that there is no obvious unified force capable of reversing those gains and then governing the territory.How a rebel movement built a modern arsenalThe Houthis Saudi Arabia first fought in 2015 were a very different force from the one now threatening the Red Sea.When the movement seized Sanaa in 2014, it inherited large quantities of weapons from Yemen's collapsing military, including Soviet-era missiles and other ageing systems. The Houthis had fighters, experience and a huge stock of weapons, but they were still primarily a local insurgency.A decade of war changed that.The Houthis received training and technical assistance from Iran and Hezbollah, while adapting their tactics through years of fighting. A 2025 UN report found evidence of both domestic weapons production and Iranian technical assistance, while Reuters reported this week that the group now has an estimated 350,000 fighters.Iran remains crucial, particularly for sophisticated missile technology and key components. But the Houthis have become increasingly capable of assembling and producing weapons inside Yemen. According to The New York Times, larger components such as missile chassis are now manufactured in Houthi-controlled territory, while parts can be sourced through complex international smuggling networks.That has made the group harder to cripple through sanctions, blockades or attacks on individual weapons shipments. Components can be moved separately through commercial supply chains and assembled later.The result is an arsenal that bears little resemblance to the force Saudi Arabia encountered at the start of the war. Houthi ballistic missiles have reached Israel, more than 1,000 miles away, while anti-ship missiles and naval drones have allowed the group to threaten commercial vessels in the Red Sea. Drones have also become an increasingly important part of its battlefield operations inside Yemen.The Houthis are also experimenting with newer technologies. The New York Times reported that an Anthropic investigation identified a group in northern Yemen using AI tools in an effort to develop guided weapons. Anthropic said there was no evidence that an operational weapon had ultimately been produced, but the episode showed the group's willingness to use new technology to expand its capabilities.There is another source of strength: the battlefield itself. Years of fighting have given the Houthis experience in missile warfare, drones, infiltration, mining and attacks on shipping. The 2022 ceasefire then gave them time to regroup, recruit and expand their military infrastructure.Their recent advance has added another advantage. As Saudi-backed forces retreated from the Red Sea coast, they abandoned or lost American- and Saudi-supplied vehicles, weapons and other equipment. Reuters reported that the Houthis captured some of this hardware during their advance.The transformation is therefore not simply about getting more weapons from Iran. It is about learning how to make, modify, smuggle, deploy and replace them.That is what makes the Houthis such a difficult opponent for Saudi Arabia. Riyadh is no longer fighting a lightly armed mountain insurgency. It is confronting a battle-hardened military organisation with domestic production networks, a large pool of fighters, long-range strike capabilities and a decade of experience adapting to a far richer enemyThe Saudi-UAE rivalry has made the problem worseOne of the most damaging weaknesses in the anti-Houthi camp has been the rivalry between Saudi Arabia and the UAE.Both countries entered the Yemen war on the same side, but their interests in Yemen have never been identical.Saudi Arabia has generally wanted a Yemeni government capable of maintaining the country's territorial unity and preventing a hostile force from controlling the north.The UAE has built strong relationships with southern forces, including the Southern Transitional Council, which supports southern independence.Those competing interests have repeatedly produced tensions within the anti-Houthi camp.Saudi Arabia has also sought to strengthen its own preferred Yemeni partners, including Islah-linked forces, while trying to limit the influence of groups backed by Abu Dhabi.The result has been a complicated network of alliances in which forces that share an enemy do not necessarily share the same political objective.For the Houthis, that fragmentation is an advantage.A united opponent could concentrate its military strength against Houthi positions. A divided one has to constantly balance the Houthi threat against disputes among its own members.This is perhaps the clearest explanation for why Saudi military superiority has produced such limited results.The kingdom has powerful weapons. It has not had a powerful, unified political partner in Yemen.A problem for MBS and Vision 2030For Mohammed bin Salman, the timing could hardly be more difficult.The central promise of Vision 2030 is that Saudi Arabia can move beyond its dependence on oil and become a major hub for tourism, technology, investment and infrastructure.That requires stability.Saudi Arabia has spent years trying to present itself as a country moving beyond the conflicts that have defined much of the Middle East. It has hosted international sporting events, expanded tourism, attracted investment and positioned itself as a major economic power.The Yemen war complicates that image.The immediate economic threat is also clear. Any prolonged disruption to oil production or export routes can affect government revenue and complicate the enormous spending required by Vision 2030.Yemen's old lessonThe deeper lesson from the Yemen war is not that military power does not matter. It is that military power has limits when there is no political structure capable of turning battlefield gains into lasting control.Saudi Arabia can destroy Houthi weapons. It can intercept missiles. It can launch devastating air strikes.What it has struggled to do is create a unified Yemeni force capable of defeating the Houthis, hold the territory afterwards and build a political settlement that the country's competing factions will accept.The Houthis, meanwhile, have used years of war to become stronger, more experienced and more deeply embedded in Yemen's political and military landscape.That leaves Riyadh facing a conflict it once expected to settle quickly but has instead helped transform into a regional security problem.The kingdom's wealth has bought it some of the world's most advanced weapons. It has not bought it an easy victory.In Yemen, geography, local politics and military adaptation have repeatedly proved more powerful than the size of a defence budget.And once again, Yemen is living up to its reputation as the place where Saudi ambitions go to die.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Shree Charani’s four-for, Shafali's quick 40 help India beat Japan in Asian Games quater-finals
articles.summary: In a stunning display of skill, India Women triumphed over Japan with an impressive eight-wicket win in the Asian Games quarter-finals. The Indian bowlers su...
articles.body:
India Women produced a dominant all-round performance to thrash Japan by eight wickets in the quarter-finals of the 2026 Asian Games, booking their place in the semi-finals against Bangladesh. The result also sets up a repeat of the Women's Asia Cup 2026 semi-final line-up, with Sri Lanka set to face Pakistan in the other last-four clash.

Shree Charani stars as Japan are bowled out for 57

After winning the toss and opting to field, India's bowlers dismantled Japan's batting line-up, restricting the hosts to just 57 in 19.5 overs. Shree Charani led the charge with a remarkable spell of 4/10, including two maiden overs, to register the best bowling figures by an Indian at the Asian Games. Shafali Verma also chipped in with two wickets for 13 runs. Ayaka Kato-Stafford top-scored for Japan with 25 off 47 balls, but the hosts struggled to build partnerships against India's disciplined attack.

Shafali and Richa wrap up chase in five overs

India's chase was emphatic, as they reached the target in just five overs, finishing at 59/2 and winning with 90 balls to spare. Shafali Verma set the tone with a blistering 40 off 15 balls, striking six fours and two sixes. She hammered four boundaries in the opening over and later sealed the victory with a six off Shimako Kato. India had promoted Kamalini and Fulmali up the order, but the move did not pay off, with Kamalini dismissed for a duck and Fulmali scoring six. Shafali then combined with Richa Ghosh, who came in at No. 4, to complete the chase in a hurry. The pair shared a warm hug after the winning hit before crossing over to greet the Japanese players. Japan's two wickets offered a small positive from an otherwise difficult outing.

articles.body: A retirement plan that began with a vacant Florida lot has now become the subject of a federal lawsuit. In 2006, Rhode Island resident Art Yatsko bought a residential lot in North Port, Florida, intending to eventually build a home there. Eighteen years later, as he prepared to begin construction, he learned that the property had been rezoned and no longer permitted a new single-family residence. According to the Institute for Justice, which represents Yatsko, the zoning change prevented him from building the home he had planned for years. Yatsko filed a federal lawsuit against the City of North Port on June 9, 2026.A retirement home planned for yearsYatsko purchased the vacant property on Kumquat Avenue in North Port in 2006 after seeing an advertisement for residential lots being offered at auction. According to the lawsuit's description, he envisioned eventually moving from Rhode Island to Florida after retirement and building a modest two or three-bedroom home. The property appealed to him because it was in a residential area and had the characteristics he wanted for his future home. He also planned to have a swimming pool, garage and space to park a small boat.For years, the lot remained undeveloped. Yatsko continued to own the property, paid taxes on it and periodically travelled to Florida to check on it. The plan was not immediate construction but a long-term retirement project. By 2024, however, he was ready to turn that plan into reality. He travelled to North Port and met with builders at the property to discuss construction and obtain estimates. It was during that process that he learned about the zoning change.The zoning rules had changedNorth Port had been revising its zoning and land-use regulations as part of an effort to encourage more commercial development. According to the Institute for Justice's account, city officials were concerned about the composition of North Port's tax base and sought to increase commercial activity. The city identified certain areas as "Activity Centers", including one near Yatsko's property, where commercial development would be encouraged. The resulting zoning designation affected vacant residential lots in the area.Yatsko's property was placed in the Commercial Office Regional (COR) zoning district. Under the new rules, a new single-family residence was no longer permitted on his lot. That created an unusual situation: existing houses remained in the surrounding neighbourhood, but Yatsko could not build a new single-family house on his vacant parcel.What can be built on the property?The dispute is not simply about whether development is allowed on the property. The central issue is which types of development the new zoning permits. According to the Institute for Justice, single-family homes are prohibited in the affected zoning district, while other uses are permitted or potentially available through different approval processes.The legal filing and the Institute for Justice's case materials point to the possibility of uses that are considerably different from the residential home Yatsko had planned. The organisation says the zoning framework could allow uses such as a nightclub or shooting range, while a conventional single-family home is prohibited. Some multifamily residential uses may also be possible with special permission. For Yatsko, however, those alternatives do not address the purpose for which he purchased the property. His plan was to build a home similar to the single-family residences already found in the neighbourhood. The dispute therefore centres on whether North Port's zoning restrictions can prevent that particular use of the vacant lot.Why the city changed the zoningNorth Port's broader planning strategy is an important part of the case. The Institute for Justice says city officials wanted to diversify the city's tax base by increasing commercial activity. Its case materials cite a city benchmark calling for commercial activity to rise from roughly 8% of the tax base to at least 18%. The city therefore created areas where commercial uses would be encouraged as part of its development strategy. Yatsko's lawyers argue that the new zoning goes beyond simply permitting additional commercial development. They contend that it also prevents some existing residential uses, including the construction of a single-family house on Yatsko's vacant property.The lawsuit also argues that the surrounding area lacks the infrastructure and development conditions needed to become the type of commercial centre envisioned by the zoning plan. Those are allegations made by Yatsko and his legal team; the city will have the opportunity to respond through the federal litigation.The constitutional challengeYatsko's lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida on June 9, 2026, under the case name Arthur Yatsko v. City of North Port, Florida. The docket identifies the action as a civil-rights case brought under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, with a jury demand.The complaint challenges North Port's zoning restrictions under the U.S. Constitution. Among the arguments described by the Institute for Justice is that the city's prohibition on a single-family home violates Yatsko's due-process and equal-protection rights. His attorneys rely in part on the U.S. Supreme Court's 1928 decision in Nectow v. Cambridge. That case involved a zoning restriction affecting a property where the proposed use was consistent with surrounding development. Yatsko's lawyers argue that the principles from that decision apply to the North Port dispute. The lawsuit does not mean Yatsko has already established that the zoning is unconstitutional. The claims will be considered through the federal court process.A dispute over one vacant lot and a wider zoning questionThe case highlights the effect that changes to local zoning rules can have on property owners who purchase land under one set of development expectations and later face different restrictions. Yatsko bought the North Port lot in 2006 and held it for nearly two decades before attempting to build. By the time he was ready to move forward, the city's revised zoning rules had changed what could legally be constructed there.For now, the property remains at the centre of an ongoing federal case. The lawsuit asks the court to examine whether North Port's restrictions on Yatsko's planned single-family home are constitutionally permissible. What began as a long-term retirement plan has therefore become a legal dispute over zoning, property use and the limits of a city's authority to regulate development.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
